frikadelle.name: Frikadelle
frikadelle.summary: A pan-fried ground-meat meatball of unknown origin, found across German, Nordic and Eastern European cuisines, with the Swedish version boiled instead.

medisterp-lse.name: Medisterpølse
medisterp-lse.summary: A traditional Danish and Norwegian sausage of finely minced pork and suet seasoned with onion, allspice, cloves, salt and pepper, first recorded in print in an early 16th-century Swedish housekeeping book.

s-pmi.name: Sápmi
s-pmi.summary: The traditional homeland of the Sámi people, spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, most of it north of the Arctic Circle.

r-dgr-d.name: Rødgrød
r-dgr-d.summary: A sweet berry pudding from Denmark and Northern Germany, whose tricky Danish pronunciation has made it a common pronunciation test since the early 1900s.

lutefisk.name: Lutefisk
lutefisk.summary: A traditional Nordic dish of dried whitefish, usually cod, cured in lye until gelatinous, historically served at Christmas feasts in Norway, Sweden and Finland.

risalamande.name: Risalamande
risalamande.summary: A traditional Danish Christmas dessert of rice pudding mixed with whipped cream, sugar, vanilla and chopped almonds, served cold with cherry sauce.

danish-golden-age.name: Danish Golden Age
danish-golden-age.summary: A period of exceptional Danish creativity, mainly in the first half of the 19th century, spanning painting, architecture, music, literature and science.

holger-drachmann.name: Holger Drachmann
holger-drachmann.summary: Danish poet, dramatist and painter (1846-1908), a member of the Skagen artists' colony and a figure of the Scandinavian Modern Breakthrough movement.

karl-madsen.name: Karl Madsen
karl-madsen.summary: Danish painter and art historian (1855-1938) closely connected to the Skagen Painters.

skagen.name: Skagen
skagen.summary: The northernmost town in Denmark, a fishing port that became famous in the late 19th century as home to an impressionist artists' colony.

sod-roof.name: Sod roof
sod-roof.summary: A traditional Scandinavian roof of sod laid over birch bark, common on rural log houses in Norway until the late 19th century; the bark, not the sod, keeps it waterproof.

romantic-nationalism.name: Romantic nationalism
romantic-nationalism.summary: A form of nationalism claiming legitimacy from a people's shared language, culture and customs rather than a monarch's authority, a central theme of Romantic-era art and politics.

christoffer-wilhelm-eckersberg.name: Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg
christoffer-wilhelm-eckersberg.summary: Danish painter (1783–1853) called the 'Father of Danish painting' for founding the Golden Age of Danish Painting.

jacques-louis-david.name: Jacques-Louis David
jacques-louis-david.summary: French Neoclassical painter (1748–1825) and supporter of the French Revolution and friend of Robespierre, famed for works like The Death of Marat.

bertel-thorvaldsen.name: Bertel Thorvaldsen
bertel-thorvaldsen.summary: Danish-Icelandic sculptor and medalist (1770-1844) who spent most of his career in Rome working in a heroic neoclassical style, later hailed as a national hero in Denmark.

peder-severin-kr-yer.name: P.S. Krøyer
peder-severin-kr-yer.summary: Norwegian-Danish painter (1851–1909) and member of the Skagen Painters, whose works are among the most expensive Danish paintings ever sold at auction.

laurits-tuxen.name: Laurits Tuxen
laurits-tuxen.summary: Danish painter and sculptor, 1853 to 1927, associated with the Skagen Painters and first head of an alternative art school to the Royal Danish Academy.

christian-skredsvig.name: Christian Skredsvig
christian-skredsvig.summary: Norwegian painter and writer (1854–1924) known for lyrical, naturalistic landscape paintings.

michael-ancher.name: Michael Ancher
michael-ancher.summary: A Danish realist painter (1849–1927) best known for depicting fishermen and the Danish fishing community of Skagen.

anna-ancher.name: Anna Ancher
anna-ancher.summary: Danish artist (1859–1935) associated with the Skagen Painters art colony, considered one of Denmark's greatest visual artists.

aalto-university-school-of-arts-design-a.name: University of Art and Design
aalto-university-school-of-arts-design-a.summary: Finland's largest art university, founded in Helsinki in 1871, which later merged with two other schools in 2010 to form Aalto University.
aalto-university-school-of-arts-design-a.source_title: Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture

constantin-hansen.name: Constantin Hansen
constantin-hansen.summary: Danish painter (1804–1880) of the Golden Age of Danish Painting, known for historical works based on Norse mythology and the painting "The Danish Constituent Assembly."

niels-laurits-h-yen.name: Niels Laurits Høyen
niels-laurits-h-yen.summary: Considered the first Danish art historian and critic (1798–1870); promoted nationalistic Danish art and shaped 19th-century Danish cultural institutions.

j-f-willumsen.name: J. F. Willumsen
j-f-willumsen.summary: A Danish painter, sculptor, graphic artist, architect and photographer (1863–1958) associated with Symbolism and Expressionism.

dalarna.name: Dalarna
dalarna.summary: A historical province in central Sweden known for its lakes, forests and strong local traditions, including a distinct dialect spoken in some western villages.

medelpad.name: Medelpad
medelpad.summary: A historical province in northern Sweden, part of Norrland, lying between its two main rivers, the Ljungan and the Indalsälven.

hassela.name: Hassela
hassela.summary: A small locality in Nordanstig Municipality, Gävleborg County, Sweden, with 364 inhabitants as of 2010.

runic-calendar.name: Runic calendar
runic-calendar.summary: A perpetual calendar using rows of runic symbols to track the days, weeks and moon phases, used in Northern Europe from the Middle Ages until the 19th century.

english-wars-scandinavia.name: English Wars
english-wars-scandinavia.summary: Napoleonic-era conflicts pitting Britain and Sweden against Denmark–Norway, starting with the 1801 Battle of Copenhagen, over Danish trade neutrality and the Danish fleet.

battle-of-copenhagen-1801.name: Battle of Copenhagen (1801)
battle-of-copenhagen-1801.summary: An 1801 battle in which a British fleet defeated a smaller Danish-Norwegian force near Copenhagen, fought after a breakdown in diplomacy over British fears of a Danish alliance with France.

first-schleswig-war.name: First Schleswig War
first-schleswig-war.summary: A war fought from 1848 to 1850 between Denmark and German-nationalist rebels in the duchy of Schleswig, ending in Danish victory with diplomatic support from Britain and Russia.

second-schleswig-war.name: Second Schleswig War
second-schleswig-war.summary: An 1864 war in which Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark over control of Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg, resulting in Denmark's cession of the duchies.

riksdag-of-the-estates.name: Riksdag of the Estates
riksdag-of-the-estates.summary: The assembled Estates of Sweden — nobility, clergy, burghers and peasants — which formed the country's highest authority next to the King until its dissolution in 1866.

scandinavism.name: Scandinavism
scandinavism.summary: A 19th-century ideology promoting cultural and political cooperation among the Scandinavian countries based on shared history, mythology and language, most popular among Danes and Swedes.

zealand.name: Zealand
zealand.summary: The largest and most populous island of Denmark, home to the capital Copenhagen, making up about 40% of the country's population.

vedb-k.name: Vedbæk
vedb-k.summary: A wealthy coastal suburb north of Copenhagen, Denmark, inhabited for at least 7,000 years and site of a Mesolithic cemetery of the Ertebølle culture.

holstein.name: Holstein
holstein.summary: A region of northern Germany between the Elbe and Eider rivers, once a county and later a duchy within the Holy Roman Empire, with Kiel as its capital.

ernst-peymann.name: Ernst Peymann
ernst-peymann.summary: Danish army officer and fortifications engineer (1737–1823) who commanded Danish forces at the 1807 Battle of Copenhagen and led the subsequent surrender talks.

battle-of-zealand-point.name: Battle of Zealand Point
battle-of-zealand-point.summary: A naval battle fought off Zealand on 22 March 1808 during the Gunboat War, in which British ships intercepted and destroyed a Danish ship of the line, the last in the Danish navy.

battle-of-lyng-r.name: Battle of Lyngør
battle-of-lyng-r.summary: 1812 battle in which a British squadron destroyed the Dano-Norwegian frigate Najaden, ending Denmark-Norway's ability to field a major warship in the Gunboat War.

gunboat-war.name: Gunboat War
gunboat-war.summary: An 1807–1814 naval conflict between Denmark-Norway and Britain, backed by Sweden, during the Napoleonic Wars, named for Denmark's tactic of using small gunboats against the Royal Navy.

k-ge.name: Køge
k-ge.summary: A Danish seaport near Copenhagen with a long history as a market town, known for its natural harbour and well-preserved old town.

arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington.name: Duke of Wellington
arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington.summary: British Army officer and statesman who served as Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief, famed for defeating Napoleon's forces after rising through campaigns in India and the Peninsular War (1769–1852).

danish-west-indies.name: Danish West Indies
danish-west-indies.summary: A Danish Caribbean colony of Saint Thomas, Saint John and Saint Croix, purchased by the United States in 1917 to become the US Virgin Islands.

danish-india.name: Danish India
danish-india.summary: The Danish forts and trading posts held in the Indian subcontinent for over 200 years, including Tharangambadi, Serampore and the Nicobar Islands, later sold to Britain.

carl-otto-m-rner.name: Carl Otto Mörner
carl-otto-m-rner.summary: Swedish courtier and member of the Diet (1781–1868), remembered for advocating Jean Baptiste Bernadotte's succession to the Swedish crown in 1810.

charles-xiv-john.name: Bernadotte
charles-xiv-john.summary: French general born Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte (1763–1844) who served as a Marshal under Napoleon before being elected Crown Prince of Sweden in 1810 and later reigning as Charles XIV John.

heligoland.name: Heligoland
heligoland.summary: A small North Sea archipelago, a Danish possession until 1807, then British until 1890, when it passed to Germany.

modern-breakthrough.name: Modern Breakthrough
modern-breakthrough.summary: A late-19th-century Scandinavian literary movement of naturalism and debate that replaced romanticism, spanning roughly 1870 to 1890 and associated with critic Georg Brandes.

henrik-ibsen.name: Henrik Ibsen
henrik-ibsen.summary: Norwegian playwright (1828 to 1906) often called "the father of modern drama," who pioneered theatrical realism in plays like A Doll's House and Ghosts.

the-wild-duck.name: The Wild Duck
the-wild-duck.summary: An 1884 play by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen about the Ekdal family, whose peace is shattered by an idealist insistent on exposing hidden truths; considered an early masterpiece of tragicomedy.

a-doll-s-house.name: A Doll's House
a-doll-s-house.summary: An 1879 play by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen about a married woman's lack of self-fulfillment, which caused controversy at the time and remains one of the world's most-performed plays.

kalevala.name: Kalevala
kalevala.summary: A 19th-century compilation of Finnish, Karelian and Ingrian folk poetry by Elias Lönnrot, regarded as Finland's national epic and influential in shaping Finnish national identity and independence.

elias-l-nnrot.name: Elias Lönnrot
elias-l-nnrot.summary: Finnish doctor and philologist who compiled the national epic Kalevala from oral folk poetry he gathered on expeditions, first published in 1835.

joik.name: Joik
joik.summary: Traditional Sámi song form from Northern Europe, in which each performance is meant to reflect or evoke a specific person, animal or place.

georg-brandes.name: Georg Brandes
georg-brandes.summary: Danish critic and scholar (1842–1927) who shaped Scandinavian and European literature from the 1870s on, defining the 'Modern Breakthrough' and co-founding the newspaper Politiken.

aleksis-kivi.name: Aleksis Kivi
aleksis-kivi.summary: Finnish writer (1834–1872) who wrote Seven Brothers (1870), the first major novel in Finnish, and is considered Finland's national writer.

johan-turi.name: Johan Turi
johan-turi.summary: First Sami author to publish a secular work in a Sami language, born in Kautokeino, Norway, in 1854; the art student Emilie Demant Hatt met him in 1904 and later helped him write his manuscript.

northern-s-mi.name: Northern Sámi
northern-s-mi.summary: The most widely spoken of the Sámi languages, spoken across the northern parts of Norway, Sweden and Finland.

adam-oehlenschl-ger.name: Adam Oehlenschläger
adam-oehlenschl-ger.summary: Danish poet and playwright (1779–1850) who introduced Romanticism to Danish literature and wrote the lyrics to Denmark's national anthem.

golden-horns-of-gallehus.name: Golden Horns of Gallehus
golden-horns-of-gallehus.summary: Two elaborately decorated 5th-century gold horns found in Southern Jutland, Denmark, in 1639 and 1734, stolen and melted down in 1802 and known today only through replicas.

viking-revival.name: Viking revival
viking-revival.summary: A late-18th- and 19th-century movement of renewed, often romanticized interest in Viking history and culture, part of the broader Romantic era.

pedar-jalvi.name: Pedar Jalvi
pedar-jalvi.summary: Finland's first Sámi writer (1888–1916), often called the principal figure of Sámi literature, whose first book, Muohtačalmmit (Snowflakes), was published in 1915.

john-stuart-mill.name: John Stuart Mill
john-stuart-mill.summary: English philosopher and politician (1806–1873), a leading liberal thinker who championed individual liberty, women's rights and utilitarianism, author of On Liberty.

the-subjection-of-women.name: The Subjection of Women
the-subjection-of-women.summary: 1869 essay by John Stuart Mill, developed with his wife Harriet Taylor Mill, arguing for equality between the sexes at a time this defied conventional norms.

anders-larsen.name: Anders Larsen
anders-larsen.summary: A Sami teacher, journalist and writer (1870–1949) who edited a Sami newspaper and, in 1912, self-published the first Sami novel, Bæivve-Alggo (Dawn).

carl-christian-rafn.name: Carl Christian Rafn
carl-christian-rafn.summary: Danish historian and antiquarian (1795–1864) who translated Old Norse literature and was an early advocate for the theory of Norse colonization of North America.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

j-nas-hallgr-msson.name: Jónas Hallgrímsson
j-nas-hallgr-msson.summary: Icelandic poet, writer and naturalist (1807–1845) who founded the journal Fjölnir to promote Icelandic nationalism; remains one of Iceland's most beloved poets.

friedrich-georg-wilhelm-von-struve.name: Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve
friedrich-georg-wilhelm-von-struve.summary: A Baltic German astronomer and geodesist known for studying double stars and starting the triangulation survey later named the Struve Geodetic Arc.

hammerfest.name: Hammerfest
hammerfest.summary: A town in Finnmark, Norway, with an ice-free harbour, known for its midnight sun in summer and polar night in winter.

hans-christian-rsted.name: Hans Christian Ørsted
hans-christian-rsted.summary: Danish chemist and physicist (1777–1851) and leader of the Danish Golden Age; his brother Anders Sandøe Ørsted later served as Danish prime minister from 1853 to 1854.

amp-re-s-circuital-law.name: Oersted's law
amp-re-s-circuital-law.summary: An alternate name for Ampère's circuital law, which relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through it, inspired by Ørsted's 1820 discovery.

hans-christian-andersen.name: Hans Christian Andersen
hans-christian-andersen.summary: A Danish writer (1805–1875) best known for 156 literary fairy tales, including 'The Little Mermaid' and 'The Ugly Duckling,' translated into over 125 languages.

niels-henrik-abel.name: Niels Henrik Abel
niels-henrik-abel.summary: Norwegian mathematician (1802–1829) who proved the general quintic equation cannot be solved in radicals, ending a problem unresolved for over 250 years, and died of tuberculosis at 26.

quintic-equation.name: Quintic equation
quintic-equation.summary: A polynomial equation of degree five, of the form ax⁵+bx⁴+cx³+dx²+ex+f=0 with a not zero, defining a corresponding quintic function.

niels-ryberg-finsen.name: Niels Ryberg Finsen
niels-ryberg-finsen.summary: Physician and scientist (1860–1904) who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Medicine for treating diseases, especially lupus vulgaris, with concentrated light radiation.

lupus-vulgaris.name: Lupus vulgaris
lupus-vulgaris.summary: A painful skin form of tuberculosis causing nodular lesions, usually on the face, that can develop into disfiguring ulcers if left untreated.

alfred-nobel.name: Alfred Nobel
alfred-nobel.summary: Swedish chemist, inventor and businessman, 1833 to 1896, who patented dynamite and later invented gelignite and ballistite, holding 355 patents in his lifetime.

gelignite.name: Gelignite
gelignite.summary: A stable, moldable explosive made of nitrocellulose dissolved in nitroglycerine, invented by Alfred Nobel in 1875.

ballistite.name: Ballistite
ballistite.summary: A smokeless propellant explosive made from nitrocellulose and nitroglycerine, developed and patented by Alfred Nobel in the late 19th century.

tartu-observatory.name: Tartu Observatory
tartu-observatory.summary: Estonia's largest astronomical observatory, historically tied to astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve and the first reference point of his geodetic arc.

friedrich-w-hler.name: Friedrich Wöhler
friedrich-w-hler.summary: A German chemist who first isolated pure beryllium and yttrium and whose synthesis of urea challenged the belief that only living organisms could make organic compounds.

anders-jonas-ngstr-m.name: Anders Jonas Ångström
anders-jonas-ngstr-m.summary: A Swedish physicist (1814–1874) and founder of spectroscopy, also known for studies of astrophysics, heat transfer, terrestrial magnetism and the aurora borealis.

svante-arrhenius.name: Svante Arrhenius
svante-arrhenius.summary: Swedish scientist (1859-1927) who in 1903 became the first Swede to win a Nobel Prize, and was first to link rising atmospheric carbon dioxide to Earth's warming surface temperature.

joseph-von-fraunhofer.name: Joseph von Fraunhofer
joseph-von-fraunhofer.summary: German physicist and optical lens maker (1787–1826) who invented the spectroscope and discovered the dark absorption lines in the sun's spectrum now called Fraunhofer lines.

tartu.name: Tartu
tartu.summary: Dorpat was the historical name, used from the 13th to the late 19th century, for Tartu, now Estonia's second-largest city and home to its oldest university.

carl-ferdinand-degen.name: Carl Ferdinand Degen
carl-ferdinand-degen.summary: Danish mathematician (1766–1825) noted for work in number theory who advised young Niels Henrik Abel and helped modernize mathematics teaching in Denmark-Norway.

knut-ngstr-m.name: Knut Ångström
knut-ngstr-m.summary: A Swedish physicist (1857–1910) who studied solar heat radiation and atmospheric absorption, inventing instruments like the pyrheliometer and pyrgeometer.

treaty-of-fredrikshamn.name: Treaty of Fredrikshamn
treaty-of-fredrikshamn.summary: Also called the Treaty of Hamina, this September 1809 treaty ended the Finnish War, with Sweden's General Kurt von Stedingk negotiating the Finnish territory's cession to Russia.

gustav-iv-adolf.name: Gustav IV Adolf
gustav-iv-adolf.summary: King of Sweden from 1792 until he was deposed in an 1809 coup after Russia's occupation of Finland; he was Sweden's last monarch to also rule Finland.

charles-xiii.name: Charles XIII
charles-xiii.summary: King of Sweden from 1809 and of Norway from 1814 until his death in 1818; known in Norway as Charles II, he was the younger brother of King Gustav III.

treaty-of-kiel.name: Treaty of Kiel
treaty-of-kiel.summary: A January 1814 treaty in which Denmark's Frederick VI ceded Heligoland to Britain and Norway to Sweden in exchange for Swedish Pomerania, while keeping Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands.

denmark-norway.name: Denmark-Norway
denmark-norway.summary: A real union of the kingdoms of Denmark and Norway (with Norway's overseas possessions) plus Schleswig and Holstein, lasting from the 16th to 19th centuries.

christian-viii.name: Christian Frederick
christian-viii.summary: Later King Christian VIII of Denmark (1786–1848); as Crown Prince Christian Frederick he was King of Norway in 1814.

eidsvoll.name: Eidsvoll
eidsvoll.summary: A Norwegian municipality where a constituent assembly met in 1814 to draft a liberal constitution and elect Christian Frederick king of Norway.

scandinavian-monetary-union.name: Scandinavian Monetary Union
scandinavian-monetary-union.summary: A currency union formed by Denmark and Sweden in 1873, joined by Norway in 1875, establishing a shared gold-standard krone/krona until it ended during World War I.

charles-august-crown-prince-of-sweden.name: Christian August of Augustenborg
charles-august-crown-prince-of-sweden.summary: Danish prince (1768-1810) who briefly became Sweden's adopted Crown Prince in 1810 before dying suddenly of a stroke; earlier a Danish general and governor-general of Norway.
charles-august-crown-prince-of-sweden.source_title: Charles August, Crown Prince of Sweden

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

convention-of-moss.name: Convention of Moss
convention-of-moss.summary: An 1814 ceasefire between Sweden and Norway that ended their brief war and became the basis for the personal union under Swedish king Charles XIII.

storting.name: Storting
storting.summary: The national legislature of Norway, established by the 1814 Norwegian constitution and still in operation today.

schleswig-holstein.name: Schleswig-Holstein
schleswig-holstein.summary: Northernmost German state bordering Denmark, historically a contested duchy whose disputed ownership between Danes and Germans sparked 19th-century wars and helped shape the German Empire.

franco-prussian-war.name: Franco-Prussian War
franco-prussian-war.summary: War between France and the Prussian-led North German Confederation, fought from July 1870 to January 1871, caused by France's bid to reassert dominance after Prussia's 1866 victory over Austria.

s-ren-kierkegaard.name: Søren Kierkegaard
s-ren-kierkegaard.summary: A Danish philosopher, theologian, poet and social critic (1813–1855) widely considered the first existentialist, known for stressing authenticity and personal choice in how one lives as an individual.

johan-vilhelm-snellman.name: J. V. Snellman
johan-vilhelm-snellman.summary: Finland-Swedish philosopher, journalist and statesman (1806–1881) who championed Hegelian philosophy and Finnish national identity, and as a senator carried through a monetary reform pegging Finland's currency to silver.

georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.name: Hegel
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.summary: German philosopher (1770–1831) and major figure in German idealism, whose dialectical system, 'absolute idealism,' shaped modern metaphysics, political philosophy and philosophy of religion.

german-idealism.name: German idealism
german-idealism.summary: A philosophical movement in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, developed from Kant's work and including Fichte, Schelling and Hegel.

church-of-denmark.name: Church of Denmark
church-of-denmark.summary: Denmark's established Evangelical Lutheran national church, headed by the monarch and Parliament, with about 70% of Danes as members as of 2026.

arvi-grotenfelt.name: Arvi Grotenfelt
arvi-grotenfelt.summary: Finnish philosopher and psychologist (1863–1941), a founder of the Finnish Science Academy and chairman of the Finnish Philosophical Society.

neo-kantianism.name: Neo-Kantianism
neo-kantianism.summary: A late modern revival of Immanuel Kant's 18th-century philosophy that sought to develop and clarify his ideas, particularly the thing-in-itself and his moral philosophy.

church-of-sweden.name: Church of Sweden
church-of-sweden.summary: Sweden's largest Christian denomination and former state church, a high-church Lutheran body headquartered in Uppsala and led by its archbishop.

edvard-westermarck.name: Edvard Westermarck
edvard-westermarck.summary: A Finnish social anthropologist, sociologist and philosopher (1862-1939) known for work on the history of marriage and the origin of moral ideas, and for the 'Westermarck effect' theory.

tune-ship.name: Tune ship
tune-ship.summary: A Viking longship of the broad-hulled karve type, built around AD 900 and excavated from a Norwegian burial mound in 1867.

stfold.name: Østfold
stfold.summary: A county in eastern Norway where the Tune ship, the first Viking ship ever unearthed, was excavated in 1867.

h-rider-haggard.name: H. Rider Haggard
h-rider-haggard.summary: English writer of adventure fiction (1856–1925), a pioneer of the 'lost world' genre best known for King Solomon's Mines and the Allan Quatermain stories.

eric-brighteyes.name: Eric Brighteyes
eric-brighteyes.summary: An 1891 epic Viking novel by H. Rider Haggard set in 10th-century Iceland, following the adventures of its title character.

george-webbe-dasent.name: George Webbe Dasent
george-webbe-dasent.summary: British lawyer, translator of folk tales, and contributor to The Times, who lived from 1817 to 1896.

gokstad-ship.name: Gokstad ship
gokstad-ship.summary: 9th-century Viking longship found in a Norwegian burial mound, the largest preserved Viking ship in Norway, now displayed in Oslo.

clinker-boat-building.name: Clinker-built
clinker-boat-building.summary: Boat-building method, originating in Northern Europe around 310–320 AD, where hull planks overlap along their edges; used by Anglo-Saxons, Frisians and Scandinavians.

walter-scott.name: Walter Scott
walter-scott.summary: A Scottish novelist, poet and historian (1771–1832), famed for his Waverley novels and narrative poems such as Marmion, credited with establishing the historical novel as a genre.

harold-the-dauntless.name: Harold the Dauntless
harold-the-dauntless.summary: Narrative poem in six cantos by Walter Scott, published in 1817, about Harold's rejection of his father's Christian conversion and his eventual redemption.
